content.intro: This lesson covers Unsafe Traits and Unsafe Implementations. It sits in Module 20, Unsafe Rust and Foreign Function Interfaces, and builds toward a practical Rust mental model rather than memorizing a term in isolation.
content.why_it_matters: Unsafe Traits and Unsafe Implementations matters when you work with reusable abstractions and type constraints. Understanding the rule helps you predict compiler or runtime behavior, document assumptions, and choose a safer implementation when inputs or system conditions change.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Generics and traits let code express reusable behavior with compile-time type checking. Rust can use static dispatch for generic parameters or dynamic dispatch through trait objects.

content_blocks.title: A reliable way to reason about it
content_blocks.text: For Unsafe Traits and Unsafe Implementations, write down the inputs, the guarantee you expect, and the boundary where that guarantee stops. Work through a minimal example first; then deliberately test one edge case. Treat every unsafe block as a contract with the reader: state the invariants, minimize its scope, and test the safe abstraction built around it.

content_blocks.text: Do not assume Unsafe Traits and Unsafe Implementations guarantees more than it actually does. Reduce a failure to a small reproducer, read the full compiler diagnostic or error value, consult the matching official reference, and change one assumption at a time.
